In diesen Verbindungen sind die einzelnen Vokale getrennt zu sprechen. In der Regel hat der zweite Vokal den dynamischen Akzent. [p. 147] Su, [scanned for '§ 9.'] Intonation kommt im /kposo [scanned for 'Ikposo'] vor. Der Hochton ist mit ” [acute] und der Tiefton mit * [grave] bezeichnet. [p. 631, on the preterite infix a-/e-] ... stets den Vokal des Pron. Sg. 1, 2 und 3 vollstandig verdrangt und von Sg. 2 und 3 blo[ß] die Tonakzente (d. i. hier der Reihenfolge nach: Tief- und Hochton) annimmt. [Soubrier 2007:40-41] Un autre ton modulé – montant – apparaît également fréquemment dans les données. Mais on peut le considérer comme une variante du ton haut. En effet, il n'apparaît pratiquement que sur des verbes non préfixés par des marques de personnes et de temps-aspect ... Dans ce cas, le rôle de ce ton modulé montant pourrait être avant tout démarcatif. [Soubrier 2007:44] La majorité des noms de la catégorie HL provient de l'anglais. ... En effet, l'accent tonique de l'anglais sur la premier syllabe d'un nom est typiquement rendu dans une langue à tons par le schème HL. [Dozeman & Koufedji 2015:5] L'ikposso comme la plupart des langues africaines est une langue tonale, c'est-à-dire c'est le ton qui donne le sens au mot.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Ikposo (ikpo1238) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Barnes et al. 2012 (accentual peaks vs plateaux), is attached to Ikposo by Glottolog only through a 'computerized assignment from \"plateaux\"' (verified on the Glottolog record) and is a closed-access pitch accent perception chapter unrelated to this language: not relevant, priority none. Beyond the item list I located and read three open first-hand descriptions: Wolf 1909 (Anthropos 4, archive.org scanned) says tone ('Intonation', high vs low) occurs in Ikposo and that within vowel sequences 'in der Regel hat der zweite Vokal den dynamischen Akzent' (p. 146), which is the only stress remark found; Anderson 1999 (SAL 28(2), open access) describes 3-4 level tones and never mentions stress; Soubrier 2007 (M2 thesis, open on the DDL site) describes 3 (4 after H) tone levels and mentions 'accent' only for English loanwords mapped to an HL scheme. Soubrier 2013 (552-pp Lyon 2 PhD, the reference grammar) remains unreachable: theses.fr redirects to theses.univ-lyon2.fr which timed out again; only its abstract ('four level tones in Uwi', nothing on stress) was read. It is the high-priority acquisition. Everything downloaded is under with.fr, HAL, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, archive.org and the DDL lab site directly.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikposo is a tone language (Wolf 1909 §9; Anderson 1999: three level tones H/M/L plus a lower-mid after H; Soubrier 2007/2013: four level tones in the Uwi dialect). The only stress remark in any accessible description is Wolf's 1909 note that in a sequence of two heterosyllabic vowels the second vowel normally carries the dynamic (intensity) accent. No source opened gives a rule for where word-level stress falls, and the modern descriptions (Anderson 1999, Soubrier 2007, SIL 2015) do not mention stress at all.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Wolf hedges with 'in der Regel' (as a rule) but names no exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Wolf's remark covers only vowel sequences (hiatus) inside a word, not the word as a whole; it is a 1909 missionary sketch (Atakpame-area informants, 'reine Akposo-Sprache') predating any tonal analysis. Modern work treats the language purely tonally; Soubrier 2007 (p. 41) notes a rising tone on unprefixed verbs that may be 'démarcatif'.
new_statements.identity_note: Wolf 1909 describes the 'pure' Akposso of mountain villages near Atakpamé (dialect not named); Anderson 1999 and Soubrier 2007/2013 describe the Uwi dialect (Doumé); Eklo 1987 the Litimé dialect of Tomegbé; SIL 2015 uses Uwi as the written standard. All fall under ikpo1238 (Glottolog lists no dialect-level codes with separate descriptions); no differently named variety is involved.

As a rule the second vowel carries the dynamic accent. ... §9 Intonation [= tone] occurs in Ikposo. The high tone is marked with ˝ and the low tone with `.

new_statements.reading: The only first-hand mention of dynamic (stress) accent for Ikposo read in this search of works with stress in the title, and it is partial: Wolf gives no word-level stress rule, only that within heterosyllabic vowel sequences the second vowel is stressed, while he describes the language as having lexical and grammatical tone (high vs. low). All later descriptions read (Anderson 1999; Soubrier 2007; Soubrier 2013 abstract) treat Ikposo as a 3-4 level tone language and say nothing about word stress. Net: no source states a word-stress rule; the language should be treated as tonal with stress undescribed, pending Soubrier 2013 chap. 1-2.

sources.citation: Anderson, Coleen G. (1999). ATR vowel harmony in Akposso. Studies in African Linguistics 28(2): 185-214.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 2.3 Tone. While it is beyond the scope of this paper to fully describe the tonal system of Akposso, it will be helpful to understand some basic elements of Akposso tone before proceeding into the description of the vowel harmony system. Akposso has three contrastive tones, high, mid, and low. From a database of 175 monosyllabic verbs, 106 verbs form minimal pairs which include seven minimal triplets. ... Nouns also have a three way contrast between high, mid, and low. After H, however, there is a fourth level tone, a lower mid-tone. There is also a high-to-low falling tone and a high-to-mid falling tone after H.
sources.note: Silent on stress (no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' in the text). Section 2.3 'Tone' (pp. 188-189) describes Akposso (Uwi dialect) as a tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L), a fourth level 'lower mid' after H in nouns, H-L and H-M falling tones after H, plus grammatical tone in the verb and tone sandhi.

sources.citation: Soubrier, Aude (2007). Phonologie et morphologie de l'ikposo de Doumé (Togo, région des Plateaux). Mémoire de Master 2, Sciences du Langage, Université Lumière Lyon 2 (dir. Denis Creissels), 99 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: D'après mes propres données, on peut effectivement identifier 3 niveaux d'opposition en général et 4 pour les noms à la suite d'un ton H. [p. 40] ... La majorité des noms de la catégorie HL provient de l'anglais. ... En effet, l'accent tonique de l'anglais sur la premier syllabe d'un nom est typiquement rendu dans une langue à tons par le schème HL. [p. 44] — Translation: 'From my own data one can indeed identify 3 levels of opposition in general and 4 for nouns following a H tone. ... Most nouns of the HL class come from English. ... Indeed the English stress accent on the first syllable of a noun is typically rendered in a tone language by the HL scheme.'
sources.locator: chap. IV.1.1 p. 40 (tone levels); IV.2 p. 44 (loanword accent remark)
sources.note: No statement on word stress in Ikposo itself; the chapter IV 'Tonologie' (pp. 39-45) describes 3 contrastive tone levels (4 for nouns after H, following Anderson), one phonological falling tone, and lexical tone classes of disyllabic nouns. The only 'accent' remarks concern English loanwords: the English stressed initial syllable is rendered by an HL tone scheme, and in sukû 'school' the second vowel carries the tone corresponding to the English stress (p. 44). Also notes no lexical vowel length (p. 20-21). Reading: tone language; stress not described as a property of native words.
